questions.q: What are the five stages an incident moves through, according to this lesson?
options: Alert, page, deploy, test, document
Detect, triage, mitigate, resolve, review
Detect, ignore, escalate, blame, close
Log, metric, trace, alert, resolve
questions.explain: Naming these stages explicitly helps a stressed team avoid skipping one, most commonly mitigation.

questions.q: What is the key difference between mitigation and resolution?
options: Mitigation is only relevant for data-quality alerts, never pipeline-health alerts
Resolution always happens before mitigation in a real incident
They are the exact same action with two different names
Mitigation stops immediate damage right now, even imperfectly; resolution is the actual fix, which usually takes much longer
questions.explain: Mitigating first gets relief to users immediately while the real fix is still being carefully investigated.

questions.q: Why does a real incident response process often assign communication to a different person than the one doing technical mitigation?
options: Communication isn't actually necessary during a real incident
Only senior engineers are allowed to communicate during an incident
Technical mitigation always takes priority and communication can wait until it's done
So neither task starves the other of attention — one person fixes, one person keeps affected people informed
questions.explain: Even a short status update is far better than silence, and it's genuinely separate work from the technical fix.

questions.q: What does "the incident is over" actually mean, according to this lesson?
options: The moment the first alert stops firing
Once the affected users have been notified, regardless of the actual fix status
As soon as a person acknowledges the alert
Resolution has landed and verification confirms the underlying cause is fixed, not just that mitigation stopped the immediate pain
questions.explain: Calling it over too early, based only on mitigation, is how the same incident quietly recurs later.

questions.q: What commonly gets skipped when a stressed team moves too fast during an incident?
options: Detection — teams almost always skip noticing the problem
Mitigation — skipping straight from detection to resolution
Nothing is ever skipped regardless of how the team is moving
Review — teams always skip this even when not rushing
questions.explain: This means users keep suffering while someone carefully investigates the root cause with no interim relief.
